description: Urbanization. The articles in this cluster offer insights into various facets of urbanization, such as green urbanization, urban regime planning, urban nature protection, and urban sustainability projects. Ernstson and Sorlin (2013) examined ecosystem services as a technology of globalization. Drawing on case studies from Stockholm and Cape Town, the authors argued that when ecosystem services are treated as objects of calculated value in decision-making, they should be viewed as socially embedded rather than simply reflecting an objective biophysical reality. Boelens (2010) proposed an actor-relational planning approach to advocate for proactive spatial planning in an actor-oriented manner, aiming to overcome the limitations of existing planning models and promote sustainable urban planning. Blok (2013a) explored ecological valuation, underscoring the importance of considering diverse senses of ecological worth. The author combined sociology and ANT to provide a socio-political understanding of ecological worth, concluding that pragmatic sociology offers crucial insights into the various perspectives on nature’s worth in political modernity. In summary, the articles in this cluster collectively contribute to a comprehensive understanding of the challenges and opportunities associated with urban sustainability.

Practices/Tools. The articles in this cluster offer valuable insights into various sustainability practices and tools. The topics covered include certifications, reporting, farming practices, green IT, and strategic planning. Bengtsson and Gerfalk (2011) examined the effects of a sustainability initiative in a Swedish municipality from the perspective of ANT. They analyzed the implementation of a reporting and analysis system for IT-supported sustainability, and viewed reporting as an influential tool for change. Rowbottom and Locke (2016) explored the development of Integrated Reporting (IR), emphasizing the role of private standard setters and the challenges encountered during the development process. The article emphasized the tensions surrounding the implementation of IR and the need to accommodate various interests within the tool. Bear and Eden (2008) delved into the spatial aspects of Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certifications, particularly the ecolabeling scheme for promoting sustainable fisheries management. The use of ANT highlights the various actors involved, including nonhumans, and the requirements related to certification processes. Coughenour (2003) used ANT to understand the innovation and adoption of conservation cropping agriculture practices, underlining the role of social networks in shaping new Indigenous cultures of conservation tillage and cropping. To summarize, the collective insights in this cluster provide a comprehensive overview of the complexities and implications of implementing sustainability practices and tools across different fields.

Transitions. The articles in this cluster provide insights into diverse aspects and levels of transitions. The topics represented in the cluster tend to focus on energy transitions, behavioral transitions, sustainable innovations. Garud and Gehman (2012) applied the translation mechanisms of ANT to illustrate the relational perspective in the transition from internal combustion engine vehicles (ICs) to electrical vehicles (EVs). Brunori et al. (2012) focused on alternative agri-food networks where consumers play a leading role. Specifically, the authors looked at consumers’ evolving attitudes and behaviors involved in these initiatives, particularly solidarity-based purchasing groups, as niches within broader socio-technical regimes in the globalized food system. The article drew on ANT to examine how consumer participation affects purchasing and consumption routines and the subsequent adaptation of producers, collecting points, and coordinators. Van Der Schoor et al. (2016) explored the transformation of communities into energy-neutral or energy-producing communities, and the role of citizens as ‘prosumers.’ In addition, the authors presented an in-depth study of recently developed networks that challenge the established way of centralized energy decision-making. They used ANT and Social Movement Theory (SMT) to investigate these initiatives and their collective strategies. Therefore, the articles in Cluster 3 collectively contribute to a holistic understanding of the multifaceted strategies and approaches to managing and fostering sustainability transitions at various levels (e.g., niches, regimes, and landscapes).

Industry. The articles in this cluster provide insights related to various industries, particularly tourism. The topics represented in the cluster tend to focus on tourism, energy, agriculture, and, recently, technology industries. Jenkins (2000) explored the role of ANT in emphasizing the link between traditional cultures (in which rural tourism is one of the products and services with a cultural component), territoriality, and sustainability. Dedeke (2017) examined the utilization of ANT to establish a sustainable tourism venture in the Amazon forest. The article investigated how a principal actor successfully created a sustainable tourism business by deploying the translation phases of ANT (including problematization, obligatory passage point, interessement, enrollment, mobilization, and black-boxing) in which equal analytical treatment is given to the human and nonhuman elements of ecoinnovation. Buijtendijk et al. (2018) studied eco-innovation in the Dutch travel industry. The article reflects the relevance of ANT in understanding the implications of eco-innovation for sustainable tourism transitions. Kaasinen et al. (2022) argued that the design of fluid and resilient human-machine teamwork must consider humans’ cognitive and physical abilities, preferences, and motivations. Based on ANT, they underscored the need for continuous co-evolution of human-machine teams to meet the changing demands and challenges of Industry 5.0. Overall, the articles in Cluster 4 contribute to deepening knowledge and practical implications concerning the nature and complexity of relationships among actants in important industries impacting sustainability. Finally, a co-word analysis was conducted to enrich the understanding of these four thematic clusters and forecast future research (Donthu et al. 2021) on ANT-based applications in sustainability.
